responseSet.title: Some Factors Influencing the Placement of a Child in Treatment
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Some Factors Influencing the Placement of a Child in Treatment

John Bremner

John Bremner

John Bremner  

This paper was given at one of the weekly general conferences of the Department of Psychological Medicine at The Hospital for Sick Children, Great Ormond Street, which are attended by a number of people belonging to different disciplines. There are many factors which ought to be considered when deciding on the disposal of a child who has been referred for psychiatric help. This paper was a review of these factors, aimed at showing and stimulating thought about the complexity of the problem, rather than discussing in depth any particular form of disposal or treatment. It was an attempt to raise questions rather than to answer them and represents no more than one way of looking at a very complex problem.

In practice we are always concerned with a child as an individual. When we think about whether a particular child should be placed in treatment, probably the first consideration which comes to mind is the needs of this child who has been brought to see us, or about whom we are being consulted. This however, is not the only consideration, for this child is a member of a social group within wider groups, and we ourselves are members of groups within wider groups. We all know this, and I have the feeling we very often forget it. If I am right then perhaps this group factor is the first factor we should consider.

We are familiar with the sort of remark that some teachers will write on a report: “Peter will do better when he learns to concentrate”; or with the parent who says—as was actually said to me once—“Peter is lazy. You can't get him interested in anything. He spends hours in his room listening to pop records. I want him to be a normal boy so he can take over my business after me.” In this instance the problem has been placed firmly on Peter's shoulders and teacher and parent have said in effect, “This is nothing to do with us, it is to do with Peter.” Therapy begins, or should begin at this point with the consultant asking those sort of questions which will enable those concerned to see the problem as having wider roots, and here the manner in which the history is taken can help enormously.

responseSet.title: The First Year of Analysis of a Fatherless Boy
responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The First Year of Analysis of a Fatherless Boy

Elsa First

Elsa First

Elsa First  

This is a report on some clinical material from the first year of analysis of a fatherless five-year-old boy. While it presents only the first stage of an ongoing analysis, this material may be of interest for the views it afforded of the impact of having a dead father on the phallic-oedipal development of a five-year-old boy whom the analytic situation seemed to have helped towards a revival of abandoned phallic-oedipal strivings. Another interesting aspect of this case which can, I hope, be noted in this material, (though it was only to come into clearer focus later in the analysis)—is the disturbance in the capacity for object relationships in a child for whom all relationships are fraught with an unbearable degree of anticipation of object loss.

History and Background

Robert L. was five years four months old when he began analysis. He was seen on four consecutive days weekly, and his mother had fortnightly interviews with the therapist. Robert's analysis was undertaken in the setting of an outpatient children's clinic which had as the centre of its research, training, and service facilities a small Therapeutic Nursery School with separate classes for three, four and five year olds, of which Robert had been a member since joining the pre-nursery playgroup at age two-and-a-half. Robert thus entered analysis in an almost communal setting in which it was reassuringly ordinary to have a “special appointment lady”. And his therapist also had the benefit of abundant observational and diagnostic material from Robert's previous years in the Nursery as well as of ongoing communications with his teachers.*

Perhaps the most significant aspect of Robert's early life was the combination of a great deal of stimulation from a large variety of intermittently available people together with repeated experiences of temporary or permanent object loss.

Robert was the only child of what was for both parents a second marriage after prior divorces. Robert's father, who had been quite active and successful in his profession, fell ill of a blood dyscrasia when Robert was six months old, and died when Robert was nineteen months old. Robert's mother had become depressed shortly after Robert's birth, and then had been intensely preoccupied with her husband's illness. After her husband had died she had been virtually alcoholic for a period of about a year.

Dilys Daws

Dilys Daws

Dilys Daws  

This sympathetic and unsentimental account of child development and the challenge of parenthood is agreeable to read and supportive in its effect. It describes the inevitable problems of growth but reassures parents that if they can be dependable and “understanding but not over-involved or fussed when difficulties arise, children have a good chance of solving the problems of development, but each child will find his own personal solution”.

The value of this book lies in its relating of all stages of life to each other, never losing sight of the way in which later pains are “full of stress and the conflict of feelings first experienced in early childhood and then forgotten because they are too painful to remember.”

It will help parents by its descriptions of the strength of the loves and hates of childhood, of the normality of these passions, and of the need to temper them in growing up. “Ultimately love and aggression, the two great forces in human life, have to find a balance between them for peace of mind and efficiency in later life”.

In showing how this balance is gradually achieved, the Author captures the flavour of each period of childhood and helps the parent to see what real needs underlie the child's behaviour at each stage. The four-year-old in a tantrum may need not only acceptance of the violence in himself, but also help in checking his anger; not the angry response he seems determined to evoke. When he continually has excuses for getting into bed at night with his parents the reassurance he really needs may be that they will not allow their relationship to be divided by him. The adolescent who flaunts rebellion as part of his dependent tie to his parents needs to be helped to a genuine independence and not allowed the false support of working through this new identity still in relation to them.

Mary Essex

Mary Essex

Mary Essex  

This series of mini books for parents on Your Child, year by year, is brilliant in design and conception and exceptionally successful in execution. Without shadow of doubt these attractive, inexpensive, easily available, easy to read little paperbacks will make an outstanding contribution to the mental health of parents and children in the next decades. As stated in each volume, the series was planned and written by a team of six Child Psychologists and Child Psychotherapists from the internationally famous Tavistock Clinic's Department for Parents and Children. Each of the fourteen books is addressed directly to parents. Each is interesting, informative, illuminating, and reassuringly realistic about the fact of life that “there must always be a lot of uncertainty in bringing up children.” Because every year of life under twelve rates a book in its own right, the importance and the achievements of becoming 3, or 5, or 7, or 9 are highlighted and dramatised. A book-for-each-year also makes it less likely that parents will treat their children “as much alike as possible” for purposes of convenience, peace at any price, or what is often felt to be “fairness”.

In general terms the books have been written to help parents understand and learn to appreciate “what lies behind” the way the baby, the child, the adolescent, the mother or the father is behaving-and-feeling at any particular time of happiness, joy, or triumph—or discouragement, despair, or anxiety. More specifically the authors state their aims in these words: “We hope parents will learn to see things which they would not otherwise observe.” “What we really hope to do is to increase your understanding because we think you, the parents, will find the best solutions yourselves.” “We would also like to feel that we helped you look again at some of the occasions when, for expediency, you did something that you knew in your heart was unfair,”

There is little question that these hopes will be realised. Hundreds of parents already wish they could have known earlier what they feel they are beginning to learn now. In the opinion of this reviewer who has discussed these books with many groups and individuals, older children and teenagers should be invited and encouraged to read for themselves what has been written for their parents about “Your 12-14 Year Old” and “Your Teenager.”

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

Transference in Daily and Weekly Treatment**

In Collaboration with Psycho-Therapists on the Staff at the Hampstead Clinic

E. Mason

E. Mason

E. Mason  

In so far as we assume that all later relationships in life are based on the earliest object ties, e.g. that of the baby to the mother, the term transference can be applied to all relationships.

Transference, in this generalised sense, is present in the adult patient's first contact with the therapist, who represents a parental figure to him, and towards whom he resumes the role of the child. He also brings to analysis, however, certain ideas and expectations with regard to treatment: he feels ill, comes for help, and welcomes the analyst as a helpmate, realising his knowledge and skill and trusting himself and his neurosis to his handling. This attitude soon disappears; the analyst becomes a loved or hated object, friendly or hostile. He takes on aspects of important people in the patient's childhood, of his early love objects; irrational elements are thus introduced into a reality situation by the past life of the patient. We would like to reserve the term transference for these manifestations, in contrast to transference in its widest sense which applies to any number of life situations, is not specific to the treatment situation and the therapist and the exact origin of which can only be assumed or guessed at. In treatment the patient's fantasies about the therapist and his irrational attitudes towards him, based on his early object relationships, distort the reality aspect of the treatment situation and enable patient and analyst to gain insight into the nature and origin of early emotional conflicts. Gradually, the patient transforms his current neurosis into a transference neurosis, that is, he transfers his emotional involvement with his parents, in its entirety, to the person of the analyst.

In the analysis of adults we work all along with that part of the patient's personality which is rational and reality adapted, and step by step confront his ego with the irrational aspects stemming from his childhood conflicts and brought into treatment in the transference.

[[RunningHead]]

Acting Out: Some Notes on Work with an Adolescent Girl and a Boy in the Latency Period

Rolene Szur

Rolene Szur

Rolene Szur  

Introduction

When in the opening years of the century a young woman, referred to as Dora, prematurely broke off her analysis, Freud wrote that his patient had taken her revenge on him, deserting him, as she believed herself to have been deserted and betrayed by her friend, Herr K. In his paper, “A Case of Hysteria” published in 1905 we find the sentence “Thus she acted out an essential part of her recollections and phantasies instead of reproducing it in her treatment”. Later, in the paper entitled “Remembering, Repeating, and Working Through” (1914) this idea was further developed, and acting out was equated with the compulsion to repeat. “We soon perceive”, he wrote, “that the transference is itself only a piece of repetition, and that the repetition is a transference of the forgotten past not only on to the doctor, but also on to all the other aspects of the current situation. We must be prepared to find, therefore, that the patient yields to the compulsion to repeat, which now replaces the impulsion to remember ……not only in his personal attitude to his doctor but also in every other activity.” He adds that: “The greater the resistance, the more extensively will acting out (repetition) replace remembering”, and concludes that in drawing attention to the compulsion to repeat, “we have only made it clear that the patient's state of being ill cannot cease with the beginning of his analysis”.

In his original formulations, therefore, Freud's concept included the ideas of (1) a necessary and inevitable element in the transference, but (2) a phenomenon which served the resistance. (3) He regarded it as taking place within the session, and (4) also outside, where he linked it with the fact that “in the course of treatment new and deeper-lying instinctual impulses, which had not hitherto made themselves felt”, might come to be repeated.

Finally he considered the dangers to the patient which might follow, and while stressing that it was mainly through the handling of the transference that impulses could be drawn into the psychic field and out of the sphere of action, he recommended in addition certain prohibitions with regard to major decisions only. For the rest, he reminded his readers that people learned only through their own experience and, sometimes harsh, mistakes.

Martha Harris, B.A.: Inside Information on Understanding Infants, (Birth to 5 Years)., A paperback published by the Dickens Press, price 5s. 0d.

E. Mason

E. Mason

E. Mason  

In this little book Mrs. Harris has undertaken the enormous task of covering in 61 short sections varying in length from one-half to four pages “those aspects of infant development to school starting age which she considers of special importance”. Her stated subject is the relationship between parents and their rapidly growing child and the questions and feelings which this evokes. These she deals with helpfully and sympathetically in the examples which form the greater proportion of the book.

Some idea of the scope of this book can be gained from the list of contents; there are nine Parts, each sub-divided sometimes into as many as ten short sections. The headings are—Parenthood; The new baby's point of view; Coming up to six months; Weaning; The toddler stage; Encouraging growth; Brothers and sisters; The young child's education; Various problems. In covering such a wide field in so short a space there is of course bound to be a temptation to compress psychoanalytic theories in such a way that I would think they can become almost meaningless or even alarming to uninformed parents. Thus love, hostility, guilt and sadness are covered in half a page which leaves “hostility”, I would think, an unacceptable concept to the ordinary devoted mother because of the associations to such a word. Mrs. Harris begins one section “For the infant, his bodily products are invested with all kinds of omnipotent powers, both terrible and highly idealised”. This difficult sentence introduces a very lucid account of the relation between physical pain and “a nasty feeling” and the ways in which the child relieves himself of both by expelling wind, flatus, faeces and urine, and how this contributes to a feeling of omnipotence which is his defence against helplessness. I would think that the first theoretical statement and other similar statements in this book could well be omitted without loss.

In the last part on “Various problems” Mrs. Harris includes a rather cursory account of Sexuality in the Young Child and Explaining Death which, like most of us, she doesn't attempt to explain. However she then gives an excellent example of a child's worries and guilt about the death of his baby sister and the need for help in bearing this situation.

[[RunningHead]]

Conceptual Problems of Acting out in Children

Alex Holder

Alex Holder

Alex Holder  

Introduction

Psychoanalytic concepts have had a varied fate in the course of the half century or so which has elapsed since their first introduction. Some of them have retained their original precision in a changing analytical scene or have become even more refined on the basis of accumulated clinical experiences and research. Within this category we might include the conceptualization of the various phases of libidinal development, of certain defence mechanisms, the super-ego and, on the clinical side, concepts like resistance or treatment alliance, to name only a few.

Many other concepts have developed in the opposite direction, i.e. from the precise to the imprecise. They started their lives with reference to well-circumscribed areas of mental functioning or as clearly and narrowly defined clincal concepts. But subsequently they were applied to a much wider range of phenomena and thus became generalised and watered down to a point of virtual meaninglessness (cf. Sandler, J., Holder, A. and Dare, C., 1970). Anna Freud has recently (1968) made some succinct comments on these developments and she noted the following, with particular reference to the concept of acting out: “Most psycho-analytic concepts owe their origin to a particular era of analytic theory or to a particular field of clinical application or a particular stage of technical procedure. They are carried forward unaltered from there, only too frequently, regardless of changes in these fields. Notwithstanding their having been firmly rooted in their home ground, they cease to fit the changed circumstances where they lead an uneasy existence and lend themselves to all kinds of theoretical misconceptions.” (p. 165).

I feel that it is not only the danger of theoretical misconception which is at stake here but something more serious and disturbing. Acting out, like cathexis and other concepts, belong to that group of analytic terms which we tend to use rather glibly and indiscriminately, often to cover up our ignorance. When we are puzzled by a piece of behaviour, for instance—be it that of a patient, friend or colleague—we are often quick in jumping to the conclusion that “he or she is acting out something”. It feels like making a diagnosis which puts our minds at rest. That this is possible is due to the fact that acting out has become an umbrella term which shelters under itself such diverse phenomena as reliving, re-experiencing, enactment, symptomatic actions, the actions of instinct-ridden characters or impulse neurotics, and, as far as children are concerned, perfectly age-appropriate behaviour. [[RunningHead]]

Transference in Child Psychotherapy**

Dina Rosenbluth

Dina Rosenbluth

Dina Rosenbluth  

Freud's Discovery of Transference

Early in his work Freud discarded hypnosis in favour of the interpretation of unconscious conflicts, for in hypnosis the conscious, rational part of the patient, the ego, was not involved, whereas in free association and the assimilation of interpretations the ego had to take an active part in the treatment. But Freud was again disappointed when he found that even after the cause of his illness had been explained to the patient, the symptoms did not necessarily disappear. Intellectual understanding was not enough; and furthermore, patients invariably developed strong feelings of love or hate towards the analyst, which Freud at first felt to be nothing but a hindrance to the progress of their analysis.

Yet it was these strong feelings and impulses directed towards the analyst, and disproportionate as a response to his actual behaviour, which led Freud to discover that they were transferred from some earlier childhood relationship within the family to the present therapeutic relationship. Freud discovered then that patients not only remembered earlier situations of conflict and anxiety in their childhood, but always transferred these to the current situation in analysis, where they re-experienced and relived them. In fact he found that only in so far as they were thus emotionally re-experienced and understood could any real change in the patient be brought about. This necessarily involved a lengthy ‘working through’ of childhood conflicts and feelings towards the analyst, becoming fully aware of them and of their origin in relation to the parents, and gradually being able to find new solutions to these conflicts. All of this implied that a consistent interpretation of all transference manifestations had now become a central task for the analyst; far from being a hindrance to treatment Freud now came to regard transference and its interpretation as the analyst's main tool.

[[RunningHead]]

Child Psychotherapy in a Day School for Maladjusted Children**

Judith Jackson

Judith Jackson

Judith Jackson  

The work of a child psychotherapist in a day school for disturbed children is deserving of some detailed examination. Working in such a milieu differs in many respects from a child guidance clinic or hospital. It presents problems which have not been previously discussed. This paper is an attempt to consider some of these problems and stems from my experience as a child psychotherapist at a day school for maladjusted children serving disturbed children between five and fifteen years of age. Once a child is placed in such a school he usually has behind him a discouraging history of social maladaptation and developmental failure. One hopes, therefore, that a placement of this kind will not only safeguard against further failures but will also rebuild in the child a trust and belief in a “good-enough” world where he can live without overwhelming fear of others and of himself, and where he may be helped to benefit from and contribute towards the community in which he finds himself.

The child psychotherapist is primarily concerned with trying to find out how this world looks to him, i.e. in which way his view of it is distorted by his own problems, and to discover how these problems in turn interfere with good relationships and emotional growth. “Treatment” gives the child a chance to reflect on his feelings and phantasies together with a concerned grown-up, who is trying very hard to understand what is going on in the child's mind and to communicate such insight. This is not an intellectual exercise but comes about within the context of a living growing relationship in which the earliest feelings and conflicts are revived, repeated and given a second chance to find resolution.

Two misconceptions held by teaching staff require clarification. In the first place there is often a false assumption that treatment consists of the child doing as he pleases in a totally permissive setting, with some suspicion that it is a “treat”, in contrast to the serious task of learning in the classroom. Quite the opposite is true. Treatment is hard work for both therapist and child and intensely painful at times. For this reason I do not feel that it is helpful for the child to be told that therapy is something “special” and, following Dr. Meltzer's suggestion, believe that the child should be told as little as possible about the reasons for being brought to therapy or the aims of the treatment (Meltzer, 1967).
